title: Your spine would be viewed as a theory-informed, interpretive, process-oriented conceptual research architecture. Its theoretical center is stakeholder theory, operationalized through the stakeholder-salience attributes of power, legitimacy, and urgency (PLU). It uses PLU to explain how stakeholder prioritization moves through decision rights, escalation pathways, and evidence-acceptance mechanisms to shape recoverability assurance.

title: This dissertation employs stakeholder theory as its broad theoretical foundation and stakeholder-salience theory as its middle-range operational lens. Using PLU as sensitizing concepts, the study interpretively examines the process through which stakeholder prioritization shapes decision rights, escalation pathways, evidence standards, and recoverability assurance in U.S. SMEs using or adopting ITDRPaaS. The SAL → DR → ESC → AE relationship constitutes a proposed, contingency-sensitive conceptual process model rather than an established substantive theory.

title: The proposed study employs stakeholder theory as its broad theoretical foundation and stakeholder-salience theory as its middle-range operational lens. Power, legitimacy, and urgency function as sensitizing concepts for examining how organizational actors interpret and prioritize competing recovery claims. The study conceptualizes stakeholder prioritization as operating through decision-rights allocation, escalation pathways, exception authority, and evidence-acceptance practices that collectively shape recoverability assurance. Accordingly, the SAL → DR → ESC → AE relationship is positioned as a proposed, contingency-sensitive conceptual process model rather than an established theory. Through generic qualitative inquiry, critical-incident prompts, reflexive analysis, and interview–artifact triangulation, the study will examine whether empirical evidence supports, refines, extends, complicates, or contradicts the proposed governance-to-assurance mechanism.
